stories.title: KCI Technologies Moves Headquarters in Maryland With 54K SF Lease
stories.excerpt: KCI Technologies is relocating its corporate headquarters within Maryland, moving about 300 employees from Sparks to Hunt Valley. The engineering, consulting and construction firm signed a 53,344-square-foot lease at St. John Properties’ 23-acre North Park business complex, and will occupy two and a half floors at 6 North Park Drive. The firm will make the move in the second quarter of 2027. The company said it focused its search on northern Baltimore County for the sake of its employees and to remain near the Interstate 83 corridor. KCI operates nearly 70 offices across 20 states and Washington, D.C., and employs more than 2,500 people. The new lease is a return of sorts for KCI, which previously had its headquarters at 10 North Park Drive for nearly two decades beginning in the 1990s. The lease follows St. John Properties’ acquisition of North Park last summer and a subsequent $2 million improvement program. Earlier this year, Solar Gaines signed a 15,036-square-foot lease at 4 North Park to relocate its headquarters and about 40 employees. St. John Properties’ Stephanie Caronna represented the landlord, while Joe Bradley and Mark Deering of MacKenzie Commercial Real Estate Services represented KCI. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: KCI Technologies relocates 300 employees from Sparks to Hunt Valley, Maryland, Q2 2027.
53,344 SF lease at St. John Properties' North Park; strategic I-83 corridor location.
Engineering/consulting firm with 2,500+ employees across 20 states signals continued Baltimore County office demand.
stories.summary: KCI Technologies, a 2,500-person engineering and consulting firm, is moving its Maryland HQ from Sparks to Hunt Valley via a 53,344 SF lease at St. John Properties' North Park complex, with occupancy slated for Q2 2027. The relocation follows the developer's $2M improvement program at the 23-acre property and signals sustained tenant demand in the Baltimore County office market. KCI cited employee convenience and proximity to I-83 as key factors in choosing Hunt Valley, a submarket with improving infrastructure.
stories.impact: Modest positive signal for Baltimore County office and adjacent multifamily demand. A 300-person relocation is incremental, but the deal validates Northern Baltimore County as an emerging talent hub—likely to attract supporting service-sector workers and drive secondary residential demand in Hunt Valley and nearby Towson submarkets over the next 18–24 months.

stories.title: Hawkins Way JV Acquires East Village Student Housing
stories.excerpt: Hawkins Way Capital and its joint venture partner, Varde Partners, have acquired 135 E. 12th St., a student housing property located in the East Village’s prime educational district. The purchase price was reportedly $51.5 million. Previously operated as Loeb Hall, a residence hall for The New School, the property will undergo renovations and be repositioned under the FOUND Study platform. It will be the third FOUND Study property Hawkins Way has acquired in Manhattan year to date. “We’ve long been looking for the right opportunity in this neighborhood, and this property represents an ideal addition to our portfolio,” said Ross Walker, managing partner, Hawkins Way Capital. “Its location, existing student housing infrastructure and flexibility put us in an ideal position to deliver high-quality accommodations in one of the country’s strongest urban student housing markets while continuing to expand the FOUND Study platform.” If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. bullets: Hawkins Way/Varde Partners acquire 135 E. 12th St. student housing for $51.5M in East Village.
Former Loeb Hall (New School residence) repositioned under FOUND Study platform; third Manhattan acquisition YTD.
Prime East Village location near NYU, New School reflects sustained urban student housing demand and capital allocation.
stories.summary: Hawkins Way Capital and Varde Partners acquired 135 E. 12th St., a converted student housing property in Manhattan's East Village, for $51.5M. The asset, formerly operated as Loeb Hall for The New School, will be renovated and rebranded under the FOUND Study platform, marking Hawkins Way's third such acquisition in Manhattan this year. The deal underscores confidence in urban student housing fundamentals in one of the country's strongest collegiate real estate markets.
stories.impact: Capital flowing into East Village student housing signals sustained enrollment demand and high per-bed rents in Manhattan's prime educational district. Increased institutional acquisition of student-adjacent residential—particularly near NYU and New School—will tighten supply and drive pricing, making ground-up or value-add multifamily development near university nodes increasingly attractive in NYC.

stories.title: Seattle Private School Buys Site for Campus Expansion
stories.excerpt: Cristo Rey Jesuit Seattle High School, a private high school in Seattle’s Rainier Beach neighborhood, has purchased a three-acre site for $3.6 million to accommodate more students. The school at 10001 57th Ave. S. plans to break ground on a new 21,000-square-foot academic building, reported the Puget Sound Business Journal. Public47 Architects is the designer, and Exxel Pacific is the general contractor on the project. The land includes space for the school’s new 21,000-square-foot building at 10001 57th Ave. S. The Norcliffe Academic Center is scheduled to break ground in mid-September. It also includes a convent that the school is using as office space. The site is part of the St. Paul Church campus, where the school currently operates. Under a deal negotiated with the Archdiocese of Seattle, the school has the option to acquire the remaining acreage on the St. Paul campus for an additional $3.4 million. The post Seattle Private School Buys Site for Campus Expansion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cristo Rey Jesuit Seattle High School acquires 3-acre Rainier Beach site for $3.6M campus expansion.
21,000 SF academic building breaks ground mid-September; option for additional acreage at $3.4M.
Rainier Beach institutionalization signals emerging submarket infrastructure and population growth anchor.
stories.summary: Cristo Rey Jesuit Seattle High School purchased a 3-acre site in the Rainier Beach neighborhood for $3.6M to expand capacity, with a 21,000 SF academic building (Norcliffe Academic Center) breaking ground in mid-September. The school also holds an option to acquire remaining acreage on the St. Paul Church campus for an additional $3.4M, indicating confidence in long-term enrollment and area vitality. Public47 Architects and Exxel Pacific are leading design and construction.
stories.impact: Institutional capital (school expansion) in Rainier Beach signals emerging demographic tailwinds and infrastructure investment in South Seattle. Educational anchors drive population stability and family household formation—expect increased multifamily interest in this submarket, particularly family-oriented, transit-proximate product in the next 2–3 years as school capacity and reputation grow.

stories.title: Bascom Refis Historic Apartments in LA’s Westlake District
stories.excerpt: The Bascom Group, LLC has completed an $8.5-million refinancing of The Charleston Apartments, a 133-unit historic multifamily community located in the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles. Michael Derk, Daizy Gomez, Linsey Farrahi and Zack Metzner of Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation arranged the debt financing on behalf of Bascom.  The loan was provided by CalPrivate Bank, represented by SVP and senior relationship manager Anthony Lopo.  The Charleston Apartments, located at 729 S Union Ave.on the edge of Downtown Los Angeles, has a century-long history tied closely to the rapid modernization of Southern California. Built in 1924, the building has transitioned over the decades from a fashionable 1920s residence into a vital pocket of affordable housing in the Westlake/MacArthur Park district, Bascom said. Ingenious Asset Group, Inc., a Los Angeles property management & real estate firm that offers commercial and residential management & brokerage services, oversees property management at The Charleston. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. The post Bascom Refis Historic Apartments in LA’s Westlake District appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Bascom Group completes $8.5M refinance of 133-unit historic Charleston Apartments, Westlake LA.
CalPrivate Bank provided debt; Marcus & Millichap arranged; built 1924, now affordable housing stock.
Historic preservation + refi activity in Westlake/MacArthur Park reflects investor interest in stabilized, rent-controlled assets.
stories.summary: The Bascom Group secured an $8.5M refinance of The Charleston Apartments, a 133-unit historic multifamily building in Los Angeles' Westlake neighborhood, via CalPrivate Bank. Built in 1924 and now operating as an affordable housing pocket, the property serves as a critical stabilized asset in the Westlake/MacArthur Park district on the fringe of Downtown LA. Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation brokered the financing.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily development signal. Refi activity in stabilized, historic, rent-controlled stock signals passive investor appetite for yield rather than growth or repositioning. Westlake remains supply-constrained for new market-rate product due to affordability regulations and historic designations—new development opportunities are limited, favoring value-add/conversion strategies in nearby submarkets like Echo Park or Downtown LA proper.

stories.title: Law Firm Nutter Expands Tenancy at Durst’s 5 Grand Central East
stories.excerpt: The Durst Organization said Wednesday that full-service law firm Nutter is expanding its office at 5 Grand Central East to 11,438 square feet. Nutter will take the entire 25th floor, in addition to renewing the existing office space on the 27th floor. “The Manhattan office leasing market is surging, especially for Class A spaces in transit-accessible locations such as Grand Central East,” said Jody Durst, president of The Durst Organization.“Nutter’s decision to expand at 5 Grand Central East reflects the desirability of the area and Durst’s long-term investment in our buildings.” The Durst Organization was represented in-house by Tom Bow, Ashlea Aaron, Bailey Caliban and Sayo Kamara. Nutter was represented by Mike Joyce and Trevor Larkin of CBRE. Ownership is deploying $16 million in capital investments at 5 Grand Central East to bring state-of-the-art infrastructure to the building, which was rebranded from 655 Third Ave. at the end of 2025. The post Law Firm Nutter Expands Tenancy at Durst’s 5 Grand Central East appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Law firm Nutter expands to 11,438 SF at Durst's 5 Grand Central East; full 25th floor + renewal 27th.
Durst deploying $16M in capital improvements; building rebranded from 655 Third Ave. end of 2025.
Midtown East office surge signaling tenant appetite for Class A, transit-accessible Manhattan real estate.
stories.summary: Full-service law firm Nutter expanded its presence at The Durst Organization's 5 Grand Central East (formerly 655 Third Ave.) to 11,438 SF, taking the entire 25th floor and renewing space on the 27th. Durst is investing $16M in capital improvements to bring state-of-the-art infrastructure to the rebranded building. The expansion reflects strong demand for Class A, transit-accessible office space in Midtown East.
stories.impact: Marginal to multifamily. Office reabsorption in Midtown East near Grand Central signals sustained white-collar employment density and high-wage commuting patterns—positive for residential demand in transit-accessible Manhattan neighborhoods (Kips Bay, Murray Hill, Astoria LIC). However, office-to-residential conversion (not implied here) remains the more material play for residential developers in constrained NYC markets.

stories.title: Report: Chicago’s Modern Big-Box Industrial Market Gains Momentum
stories.excerpt: Chicago’s modern big-box industrial market is experiencing a resurgence in leasing activity, with 9.1 million square feet leased in the first half of 2026, a 51% year-over-year increase from 6 million square feet in the same period in 2025, according to a recent report by Cushman & Wakefield. The report highlights renewed occupier demand and improving market fundamentals, with the region seeing the strongest first-half leasing performance since 2021, reflecting demand for large-scale warehouse and distribution facilities and signaling continued momentum in the regional industrial market. Large-scale transactions have played a critical role in the market’s resurgence. Through mid-2026, six leases exceeding 500,000 square feet were completed. Third-party logistics providers remain the primary source of demand, while manufacturing users also emerged as an important contributor. Demand has been especially concentrated in newly developed facilities. Approximately 60% of leasing volume completed during the first half of 2026 occurred in facilities delivered since 2020. The post Report: Chicago’s Modern Big-Box Industrial Market Gains Momentum appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Chicago modern industrial: 9.1M SF leased H1 2026, +51% YoY vs. 6M SF in H1 2025.
Six leases >500K SF completed; ~60% of volume in facilities delivered since 2020; 3PLs leading demand.
Strongest H1 performance since 2021; manufacturing also contributing; recent supply absorbing quickly.
stories.summary: Chicago's modern big-box industrial market rebounded sharply in H1 2026, with 9.1M SF leased—a 51% year-over-year increase from 6M SF in H1 2025, per Cushman & Wakefield. Six leases exceeding 500K SF drove activity, with approximately 60% of leasing volume concentrated in facilities delivered since 2020. Third-party logistics providers remain the primary occupier, though manufacturing demand is also strengthening, signaling renewed regional distribution and supply-chain confidence.
stories.impact: Strong industrial demand in Chicago indicates regional logistics hub vitality and in-migration of supply-chain operations, likely driven by Midwest labor cost advantages and proximity to major markets. Secondary effect: industrial employment and wage-earning worker in-migration will support multifamily demand in industrial-proximate submarkets (Pilsen, Bridgeport, Far South Side); developers should target purpose-built rental housing near logistics clusters and transportation nodes.

stories.title: For U.S. Life Sciences Real Estate, 2026 Is a Tale of Stabilization
stories.excerpt: The U.S. life sciences real estate market remains oversupplied, but improving funding conditions and a sharply reduced construction pipeline are beginning to set the stage for a recovery, according to Cushman & Wakefield. Asking rents at U.S. life sciences facilities averaged $64.17 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, down 5.3 percent compared to last year, and vacancy climbed nearly 200 basis points to 24.3 percent. Cushman & Wakefield expects market rents to continue to slip, particularly in heavily supplied regions, but said stronger funding and occupier demand could stabilize rates over the next 18 to 24 months. Life sciences inventory has expanded from 171 million square feet in 2021 to 239 million square feet today, but the construction pipeline now represents only 2 percent of inventory, down from 17 percent at its mid-2023 peak. Just 1.2 million square feet was delivered through the first half of this year, which is an 82 percent decline from the first half of 2025, with future development increasingly concentrated in pre-leased and build-to-suit projects. Capital markets are also gradually reopening. R&D investment sales totaled more than $9.3 billion during the four quarters ending in June, up 4 percent from a year earlier. Deal count rose 9 percent to 292, above the prior 10-year average, although average transaction size declined 5 percent. Globally, venture capital investment reached $29.9 billion in the first half of 2026, up 30 percent from last year, and the strongest first-half showing since 2022. North America accounted for $17.9 billion, up 35 percent. IPO volume nearly tripled to $6.8 billion, while global mergers and acquisitions activity reached $97.2 billion, nearly three times its level a year earlier. San Diego County remains one of North America’s largest life sciences hubs, with 26.6 million square feet of inventory and asking rents averaging $67.09 per square foot. bullets: U.S. life sciences real estate: vacancy 24.3% (Q2 2026), asking rents $64.17/SF, down 5.3% YoY.
Inventory expanded 171M SF (2021) to 239M SF today; construction pipeline only 2% of inventory.
Funding conditions improving; market stabilization expected in 18–24 months despite persistent oversupply.
stories.summary: The U.S. life sciences real estate market remains oversupplied with 24.3% vacancy and asking rents averaging $64.17/SF in Q2 2026 (down 5.3% YoY), per Cushman & Wakefield. However, a sharp reduction in the construction pipeline (now only 2% of the 239M SF inventory) combined with improving biotech funding conditions is expected to stabilize rates over the next 18–24 months. Rents will likely continue to slip in heavily supplied regions before recovery takes hold.
stories.impact: Life sciences oversupply is a distraction for multifamily developers in biotech hubs (San Diego, Boston, Bay Area). Capital constraints on biotech tenants compress occupier demand and suppress secondary office-to-residential conversion economics. Expect continued rent pressure and lower speculative development starts in life sciences submarkets until funding cycle matures; focus instead on serving the *non-biotech* workforce in these metros (service, support, lower-wage jobs anchoring rental demand).

stories.title: AI Startup Thinking Machines Lab Takes 22K SF at 79 Fifth Avenue for First NYC Office
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence research startup Thinking Machines Lab is coming to New York. Just a year and a half after launching in San Francisco, the company has inked a 21,500-square-foot lease at Kalimian Properties’ 79 Fifth Avenue just one block west of Union Square, Commercial Observer has learned. The terms of the deal were not disclosed, but asking rents in the 18-story office building hover slightly above $100 per square foot, according to a source familiar with the deal. Thinking Machines Lab was founded in early 2025 by Mira Murati, former chief technology officer at OpenAI, to design specialized AI models and create tools for researchers and businesses to train their own models. The company achieved a $12 billion valuation in July 2025. JLL’s Justin Haber and Kyle Riker negotiated the lease on behalf of the tenant, while Newmark’s David Falk, Daniel Levine and Dylan Weisman represented the landlord. A spokesperson for JLL confirmed the lease but declined to comment on the deal. The team at Newmark did not respond to a request for comment. Thinking Machines Lab’s new East Coast home will occupy the entire fourth floor of 79 Fifth Avenue. The building between East 15th and East 16th streets is also home to consulting company Capgemini America, streaming giant Hulu, and The New School. It is also home to fashion retailer Free People on the ground floor. Kalimian Properties’ Albert Kalimian did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the deal. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: AI startup Thinking Machines Lab (Mira Murati, ex-OpenAI CTO) leases 21,500 SF at 79 Fifth Ave, NYC.
$12B valuation (July 2025); founded early 2025; first NYC office one year into operations.
Rents ~$100/SF; Union Square adjacency reflects strong appeal of Manhattan for AI research talent concentration.
stories.summary: Thinking Machines Lab, an AI research startup founded in early 2025 by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has leased 21,500 SF at Kalimian Properties' 79 Fifth Avenue, just west of Union Square. The company achieved a $12B valuation in July 2025 and is establishing its first New York office just 18 months after launch in San Francisco. Asking rents at the 18-story building hover slightly above $100/SF.
stories.impact: High-growth AI and deep-tech talent concentration in Manhattan (Union Square/Flatiron) is expanding beyond traditional finance hubs. Influx of well-funded AI firms and their high-earning employees will drive demand for premium multifamily in Union Square East/Kips Bay/Gramercy submarkets. Expect intensified competition for Class A residential targeting $3K–$5K+ monthly rents and appeal to young, high-income knowledge workers in the next 12–24 months.

stories.title: Pizza Napoli to Open in 3K SF at 383 Fifth Avenue
stories.excerpt: As one pizzeria shuts down, another is growing in its place, Commercial Observer has learned. Pizza Napoli has signed a 2,500-square-foot lease at Jonathan and Jan Soleimani’s 383 Fifth Avenue just off East 36th Street in Midtown, where asking rent started at $25,000 per month, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. The tenant signed a 15-year lease for the space, Meridian said. The site was previously the home of Famous Italian Pizza. “Fifth Avenue retail continues to show real strength for food and beverage users, and this was a straightforward reposition — pizzeria to pizzeria, minimal downtime for the landlord,” Meridian’s Noam Aziz said in a statement. “Jonathan and Jan were great partners throughout the process, and Pizza Napoli is going to do well in that location given the foot traffic on that stretch.” Aziz represented the landlords alongside Carson Shahrabani and Daniel Zacaim, while the tenant did not use any outside brokers. “When a pizzeria space turns over on Fifth Avenue, the read-through for the neighborhood is usually positive — it tells you the trade area still supports that price point and that use,” Zacaim said in a statement. “Pizza Napoli is a strong operator stepping into a location with a built-in customer base.” Pizza Napoli, which could not be reached for comment, has the potential to benefit from everyday foot traffic along Fifth Avenue, as well as from dispensary NY Cannabis Company, which is right next door. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Pizza Napoli signs 2,500 SF lease at 383 Fifth Avenue, Midtown; $25K/month; 15-year term.
Replaces Famous Italian Pizza; Fifth Avenue retail showing strength in F&B, minimal turnover.
Retail stabilization on prime Fifth Avenue signals confidence in pedestrian traffic and dining recovery.
stories.summary: Pizza Napoli has signed a 2,500 SF lease at 383 Fifth Avenue (off East 36th Street, Midtown) at $25K/month on a 15-year term, replacing the previous pizzeria tenant. The transaction reflects ongoing strength in Fifth Avenue retail, particularly for food-and-beverage users, with minimal downtime between tenants and straightforward repositioning.
stories.impact: Minimal to multifamily development. F&B tenancy strength on Fifth Avenue Midtown signals pedestrian foot traffic recovery and consumer spending, which supports surrounding daytime employment and visitor volume—modest positive indicator for full-service residential demand in Midtown East/Kips Bay, but not a primary driver of supply or economics.

stories.title: Nonprofit Biohub, Software Firm Fundraise Up Lease 20K SF at 100-104 Fifth Avenue
stories.excerpt: Two nonprofit-related tenants are moving to an office just west of Manhattan’s Union Square. In the largest deal, the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, better known simply as Biohub, secured a 10,666-square-foot lease at Sovereign Partners’ 100-104 Fifth Avenue, Commercial Observer has learned. The nonprofit biomedical research organization will occupy the entire ninth floor of the 20-story tower at the southwest corner of Fifth Avenue and West 15th Street, according to sources. The building is one block west of Union Square. Biohub was founded in 2016 by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, with the goal to cure, prevent and manage human diseases. The company currently lists offices and a research laboratory at Columbia University’s Studebaker Building at 615 West 131st Street. Sources said the move marks a relocation from a Biohub office near Union Square, but no address in the neighborhood was found. Biohub was represented by Newmark’s David Falk, Mike Courson and Dylan Weisman. Falk also represented Sovereign Partners alongside Daniel Levine and Paige Raisides. A spokesperson for Newmark did not respond to a request for comment on the transaction. The nonprofit will be in good company at the Fifth Avenue office tower. Fundraise Up, a fundraising platform designed for nonprofit organizations, has signed its own lease at the building. Fundraise Up took 9,522 square feet across the entire seventh floor, in a relocation from 219 36th Street in Brooklyn’s Industry City complex. The lease terms for both of the recent deals were not disclosed, but asking rents in the building range from $110 to $150 per square foot, according to the source. Cushman & Wakefield’s David Hoffman, Sam Hoffman and Louden Sheehan negotiated the lease on behalf of Fundraise Up. The same Newmark team represented the landlord. bullets: Chan Zuckerberg Biohub leases 10,666 SF (entire 9th floor) at Sovereign Partners' 100-104 Fifth Ave, Manhattan.
Biohub relocating within Union Square submarket; founded 2016 by Zuckerberg; biomedical research focus.
Nonprofit biomedical research institutions anchoring premium Fifth Avenue Union Square office demand.
stories.summary: The Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, a nonprofit biomedical research organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan in 2016, leased 10,666 SF (the entire ninth floor) at Sovereign Partners' 100-104 Fifth Avenue (southwest corner of Fifth and West 15th Street), one block west of Union Square. The move represents a relocation within the Union Square submarket. Biohub currently maintains offices and a lab at Columbia University's Studebaker Building in Washington Heights.
stories.impact: Nonprofit and research-intensive tenancy on premium Fifth Avenue reflects sustained institutional capital commitment to Manhattan's life sciences and biomedical research ecosystem. While not direct multifamily impact, institutional (nonprofit and university-affiliated) clustering near Union Square attracts graduate students, postdocs, and research staff—typically underserved by premium residential product. Secondary multifamily opportunity: purpose-built graduate student and postdoc housing in East Village/Kips Bay submarkets near Union Square research hubs.
